Red emergency lights bathed the control room as Solis Base quaked under the Martian dust storm. Panic flared in Maya’s chest, not from the roaring wind battering the hab module, but from the agonizing wall of static in her headset. 

Twenty minutes. That’s how long her half-spoken words would take to travel across the void to Earth, if they even made it past the ionospheric interference.

"Bypass secondary array," she muttered, her fingers flying across the console, overriding automated storm locks. "Come on, Leo..."

The rogue signal had been her lifeline. She had memorized the cadence of his voice, the way he described the Chilean night air. Hearing him speak her name had shattered months of isolation. 

A violent gust struck, and the terminal chimed: *COMMS DISH ALIGNMENT LOST.*

Through the viewport, Mars was a swirling vortex of rust. Maya bypassed the system safety limits, dumping her audio buffer into a high-powered burst aimed at South America—a blind shot into the dark.

She hit record.

"Leo," she whispered. "The storm tore the array, but I heard you. I’ve been listening every night. Don't stop looking."

She slammed transmit just as primary power failed, plunging her into darkness. 

For twenty minutes, Maya sat in the dark, watching the terminal's blue emergency battery count down. Twenty minutes for her voice to cross the ocean of space. 

When the frequency hummed back to life, it wasn't the delayed broadcast from Chile. It was a real-time feed from a supply shuttle entering Mars's upper atmosphere.

"Maya, I got tired of the delay," Leo’s voice crackled, impossibly close and clear. "I'm coming down."

Come back for the next part tomorrow.
